metate.name: Metate
metate.summary: A ground stone tool, a type of quern, traditionally used in Mesoamerica—mainly by women—to grind nixtamalized maize and other foods such as tortillas.

comal-cookware.name: Comal
comal-cookware.summary: A smooth, flat griddle used across Mexico and Central America to cook tortillas, toast spices and sear meat, often handed down through generations.

chontalpa.name: Chontalpa
chontalpa.summary: A region in the Mexican state of Tabasco, home to much of its Chontal Maya population and historically a major source of cocoa.

olmecs.name: Olmecs
olmecs.summary: An early Mesoamerican civilization that flourished roughly 1200 to 400 BC in what is now Veracruz and Tabasco, known for colossal stone heads and considered one of the cradles of civilization.

teotihuacan.name: Teotihuacan
teotihuacan.summary: An ancient Mesoamerican city near modern Mexico City, home to the Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon, likely the largest city in the Americas around 1 to 500 CE with up to 100,000 people.

pyramid-of-the-sun.name: Pyramid of the Sun
pyramid-of-the-sun.summary: The largest building at Teotihuacan, Mexico, and one of the largest in Mesoamerica, believed to have been built around 200 AD along the Avenue of the Dead.

pyramid-of-the-moon.name: Pyramid of the Moon
pyramid-of-the-moon.summary: The second-largest pyramid at Teotihuacan, Mexico, built in phases between about 100 and 450 CE over an older structure and used for ceremonies and ritual sacrifices honoring the Great Goddess.

san-lorenzo-tenochtitl-n.name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
san-lorenzo-tenochtitl-n.summary: Major Olmec city on Mexico's Gulf Coast, the leading Olmec center from about 1400 to 900 BCE and known for its colossal carved stone heads.

la-venta.name: La Venta
la-venta.summary: A pre-Columbian archaeological site of the Olmec civilization in the Mexican state of Tabasco.

izapa.name: Izapa
izapa.summary: A large pre-Columbian archaeological site in Chiapas, Mexico, best known for its occupation during the Late Formative period.

popol-vuh.name: Popol Vuh
popol-vuh.summary: Foundational sacred narrative of the Kʼicheʼ Maya people of Guatemala, containing their creation myth and history; preserved orally until it was written down around 1550.

temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.name: Temple of the Feathered Serpent
temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.summary: The third-largest pyramid at Teotihuacan in central Mexico, dated to around 150-200 CE, known for feathered-serpent carvings and more than a hundred sacrificial burials found beneath it.
temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-teotihua.source_title: Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan

kaminaljuyu.name: Kaminaljuyu
kaminaljuyu.summary: A Pre-Columbian Maya site now within Guatemala City, occupied from about 1500 BCE to 1200 CE and once among the greatest sites in the New World.

cop-n.name: Copán
cop-n.summary: An archaeological site of the Maya civilization in western Honduras, capital of a major kingdom from the 5th to 9th centuries AD until its abandonment in the early 10th century.

motagua-river.name: Motagua River
motagua-river.summary: A 486-km river in Guatemala whose valley holds jadeite deposits long used by Indigenous Mesoamerican peoples.

cancu-n.name: Cancuén
cancu-n.summary: A pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in Guatemala's Petén region, noted for having one of the largest palaces in the Maya world.

guayt-n.name: Guaytán
guayt-n.summary: A Maya archaeological site in Guatemala, inhabited from about 250 BC to 900 AD, notable for controlling a source of jadeite.

princeton-maya-vase-with-god-l.name: Princeton Vase
princeton-maya-vase-with-god-l.summary: A Late Classic Maya drinking vessel for chocolate, painted in codex style, depicting a throne scene where a bound captive is decapitated before an aged deity.
princeton-maya-vase-with-god-l.source_title: Princeton Maya Vase with God L

zapotec-civilization.name: Zapotec civilization
zapotec-civilization.summary: A pre-Columbian civilization of Mexico's Valley of Oaxaca, flourishing from about 700 BC to 1521 CE, whose city Monte Albán was one of Mesoamerica's first major urban centers.

mixtec.name: Mixtec
mixtec.summary: Indigenous Mesoamerican peoples of Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero, Mexico, whose civilization lasted from about 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest in 1523.

monte-alb-n.name: Monte Albán
monte-alb-n.summary: An ancient hilltop city in Oaxaca, Mexico, founded around 500 BCE, that served as the main political and economic center of the Zapotec civilization for nearly a thousand years.

tonin.name: Toniná
tonin.summary: A Maya city in what is now Chiapas, Mexico, known for its large pyramid and detailed stucco carvings, and for recording the last known Maya Long Count date, in 909 CE.

nahuatl.name: Nahuatl
nahuatl.summary: A language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken in central Mexico since at least the 7th century CE, once the prestige language of the Aztec Empire.

la-mojarra-stela-1.name: La Mojarra Stela 1
la-mojarra-stela-1.summary: A four-ton carved limestone monument from 156 CE, pulled from Mexico's Acula River in 1986, bearing about 535 glyphs and among the earliest known written records in Mesoamerica.

isthmian-script.name: Isthmian script
isthmian-script.summary: An early set of symbols found around the Isthmus of Tehuantepec dating from about 500 BCE to 500 CE, also called the Epi-Olmec script, whose status as true writing is disputed.

epi-olmec-culture.name: Epi-Olmec culture
epi-olmec-culture.summary: A culture of central Veracruz, Mexico, lasting roughly 300 BCE to 250 CE, successor to the Olmec and known for sophisticated calendrics and an early writing system.

cascajal-block.name: Cascajal Block
cascajal-block.summary: A tablet-sized stone slab from the early first millennium BCE bearing unknown symbols, claimed to be the earliest writing system found in the Americas and linked to the Olmec civilization.

mesoamerican-long-count-calendar.name: Long Count calendar
mesoamerican-long-count-calendar.summary: A non-repeating pre-Columbian Mesoamerican calendar, most associated with the Maya, counting days from a mythical creation date equal to 3114 BCE and widely inscribed on monuments.

palenque.name: Palenque
palenque.summary: A Maya city-state in southern Mexico, inhabited from around 226 BCE to 799 CE, known for fine architecture and inscriptions and for its ruler Pakal the Great, whose tomb was found there.

tikal.name: Tikal
tikal.summary: A ruined ancient Maya city in Guatemala's rainforest that was capital of one of the most powerful Maya kingdoms, peaking roughly between 200 and 900 CE.

terrence-kaufman.name: Terrence Kaufman
terrence-kaufman.summary: An American linguist (1937-2022) known for documenting Indigenous languages of Mexico and Central America and for work in Mesoamerican historical linguistics.

maya-script.name: Maya script
maya-script.summary: The Maya civilization's writing system, the only Mesoamerican script fully deciphered, combining logograms with syllabic glyphs; used from the 3rd century BCE until the Spanish conquest.

san-bartolo-maya-site.name: San Bartolo
san-bartolo-maya-site.summary: Small pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in northern Guatemala, famous for Late-Preclassic murals and some of the earliest known Maya writing.

tuxtla-statuette.name: Tuxtla Statuette
tuxtla-statuette.summary: A small jade figurine from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec carved with Epi-Olmec script and a Long Count calendar date, the oldest such date known when it was discovered in 1902.

naj-tunich.name: Naj Tunich
naj-tunich.summary: A series of natural caves in Guatemala used as a Maya ritual pilgrimage site, notable for Late Classic hieroglyphic texts and painted scenes.

pet-n-department.name: El Petén
pet-n-department.summary: The largest department of Guatemala, covering about a third of the country's area, with its capital at Flores.

stephen-d-houston.name: Stephen D. Houston
stephen-d-houston.summary: An American anthropologist and Mayanist (born 1958) renowned for research on Maya writing, kingship and dynastic politics, and a professor at Brown University.

michael-d-coe.name: Michael D. Coe
michael-d-coe.summary: An American archaeologist (1929–2019) and leading Mayanist known for research on Mesoamerica and popular books such as The Maya and Breaking the Maya Code.

matthew-stirling.name: Matthew Stirling
matthew-stirling.summary: American archaeologist (1896–1975) best known for excavations on Mexico's Gulf Coast that greatly advanced understanding of the Olmec civilization.

tres-zapotes.name: Tres Zapotes
tres-zapotes.summary: A Mesoamerican archaeological site in Mexico, sometimes called a third major Olmec capital, that remained a cultural center for roughly 2,000 years across several periods.

marion-stirling-pugh.name: Marion Stirling Pugh
marion-stirling-pugh.summary: American archaeologist (1911–2001) known for expeditions to Tres Zapotes with her husband Matthew Stirling; her Long Count reading on a stela helped establish the antiquity of the Olmec civilization.

zapotec-script.name: Zapotec script
zapotec-script.summary: The earliest writing system of Mesoamerica's Zapotec culture, centered on Monte Albán in Oaxaca; despite many carved stone inscriptions, it remains largely undeciphered.

isthmus-of-tehuantepec.name: Isthmus of Tehuantepec
isthmus-of-tehuantepec.summary: A narrow strip of land in Mexico marking the shortest route between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean, once a major overland transport route before the Panama Canal opened.

calakmul.name: Calakmul
calakmul.summary: A major Maya city in Mexico's Petén Basin, seat of the powerful 'Snake Kingdom' during the Classic period, with an estimated population of 50,000.

george-cowgill.name: George L. Cowgill
george-cowgill.summary: American anthropologist and archaeologist (1929–2018) whose career centred on research at the ancient Mexican city of Teotihuacán and the comparative study of early states and cities.

valley-of-mexico.name: Valley of Mexico
valley-of-mexico.summary: A large basin in the highlands of central Mexico that was home to pre-Columbian civilizations including Teotihuacan and the Aztec Empire, and now contains Mexico City.

cuicuilco.name: Cuicuilco
cuicuilco.summary: An archaeological site in the Valley of Mexico whose pyramid, begun a few centuries BCE, may make it the valley's oldest city; it was destroyed by a volcanic eruption between 245 and 315 CE.

cerro-de-las-mesas.name: Cerro de las Mesas
cerro-de-las-mesas.summary: An archaeological site in Veracruz, Mexico, a regional center from 600 BCE to 900 CE and capital from 300 to 600 CE, linked to epi-Olmec culture and holding a cache of about 800 jade objects.

dzibanche.name: Dzibanche
dzibanche.summary: An extensive Maya archaeological site in Mexico, the first capital of the Kaan (Snake) kingdom and birthplace of the powerful Kaanu'l dynasty, which dominated the Maya lowlands for two centuries.

yuknoom-ch-een-i.name: Yuknoom Ch'een I
yuknoom-ch-een-i.summary: First known Maya king (ajaw) of the Kaan kingdom, possibly the father of King Tuun K'ab' Hix.

ajaw.name: Ajaw
ajaw.summary: A pre-Columbian Maya political title meaning 'Lord,' also the name of a day in the Maya tzolk'in calendar tied to rulers' period-ending rituals.

axis-mundi.name: Axis mundi
axis-mundi.summary: A concept in comparative mythology representing a connection between heaven and earth, symbolized by trees, mountains, pillars or towers across many cultures.

olmec-religion.name: Olmec religion
olmec-religion.summary: Belief system of the Olmecs, the first Mesoamerican civilization, which lasted until about 400 BCE. No direct accounts survive, so archaeologists reconstruct it from iconography, art and comparison with later cultures.

joralemon.name: Peter David Joralemon
joralemon.summary: A writer on Olmec religion, noted among people sharing the Joralemon surname.

kinich-ahau.name: Kinich Ahau
kinich-ahau.summary: The 16th-century Yucatec name for the Maya sun god, depicted in the Classic period as a middle-aged man with an aquiline nose and filed tooth, still part of Lacandon storytelling into the 20th century.

five-suns.name: Five Suns
five-suns.summary: An Aztec and Nahua belief that the world has passed through five cycles of creation and destruction, with the current era being the fifth.

feathered-serpent.name: Feathered Serpent
feathered-serpent.summary: A supernatural deity found across Mesoamerican religions, known as Quetzalcōātl to the Aztecs and Kukulkan to the Maya, its feathers and serpent body symbolizing divine and earthly natures.

chaac.name: Chaac
chaac.summary: The Maya god of rain, thunder and lightning, who strikes clouds with a lightning axe to make them produce rain; he corresponds to the Aztec god Tlaloc.

teuchitl-n-culture.name: Teuchitlán culture
teuchitl-n-culture.summary: An archaeologically defined culture in West Mexico's Tequila Valleys, active from about 350 BCE to 450-500 CE, known for burying its dead in shaft and chamber tombs.

pet-n-basin.name: Petén
pet-n-basin.summary: A subregion of the Maya Lowlands in northern Guatemala where major Maya centers such as Tikal and Calakmul flourished.

jalisco.name: Jalisco
jalisco.summary: A state in western Mexico, home to Guadalajara, considered the origin of mariachi, tequila and ranchera music, and economically among Mexico's most important states.

amate.name: Amate
amate.summary: A type of bark paper made in Mexico since precontact times, used for Mayan and Aztec codices and records, whose production survived the Spanish conquest in remote mountain villages.

nayarit.name: Nayarit
nayarit.summary: A Mexican Pacific coast state home to Uto-Aztecan peoples such as the Huichol and Cora, exposed to Spanish conquest in the 16th century with resistance lasting until 1722.

colima.name: Colima
colima.summary: A small Mexican state on the central Pacific coast, the fourth smallest in the country, bordering the states of Jalisco and Michoacán.
